app_note: Black pepper was historically one of the most valuable global spices.
risk_note: Usually used in small amounts.

app_note: White pepper is made from ripe peppercorns with the outer layer removed.
risk_note: Flavor differs from black pepper and can be earthy.

app_note: Cayenne heat comes from capsaicinoids.
risk_note: Capsaicin sensitivity varies.

app_note: Paprika can be sweet smoked or hot depending on pepper type.
risk_note: Heat level is not obvious from the name alone.

app_note: Chili powder may be pure ground chiles or a spice blend depending on region.
risk_note: Blend ingredients may include allergens or anti-caking agents.

app_note: Cinnamon comes from tree bark and has several commercial species.
risk_note: Cassia and Ceylon differ in coumarin levels; source review needed.

app_note: Nutmeg is the seed while mace is the seed covering from the same fruit.
risk_note: Large doses can be toxic; food-use context matters.

app_note: Mace comes from the lacy covering around the nutmeg seed.
risk_note: Use neutral culinary wording.

app_note: Cloves are dried flower buds and are rich in eugenol aroma.
risk_note: Essential-oil claims should be avoided unless sourced.

app_note: Allspice is a single spice that tastes like a blend of cinnamon clove and nutmeg.
risk_note: Not the same as mixed spice.

app_note: Ginger flavor changes when dried cooked or candied.
risk_note: Wellness claims require source review.

app_note: Turmeric is both a spice and a natural color source.
risk_note: Supplement-level curcumin claims differ from food spice use.

app_note: Cumin is widely used across Middle Eastern Indian Latin American and North African cooking.
risk_note: Usually used in small amounts.

app_note: Coriander seed and cilantro leaf come from the same plant but taste different.
risk_note: Some people dislike cilantro leaf because of genetics; seed is different.

app_note: Cilantro has a genetic soap-taste divide for some people.
risk_note: Not usually a safety concern.

app_note: Parsley is more than garnish and can be a major flavor in tabbouleh.
risk_note: High vitamin K content may matter only in medical contexts.

app_note: Basil has many varieties with distinct aroma profiles.
risk_note: Usually low concern as food.

app_note: Oregano is strongly associated with Mediterranean and Mexican cuisines.
risk_note: Essential oil claims should not be inferred from herb use.

app_note: Thyme's aroma is linked to thymol and related compounds.
risk_note: Food-use amounts are distinct from essential oils.

app_note: Rosemary extracts can also be used as antioxidants in foods.
risk_note: Concentrated extracts should be tracked separately.

app_note: Sage is strongly aromatic and often paired with rich fatty foods.
risk_note: Concentrated oils differ from culinary use.

app_note: Dill weed and dill seed have different flavor profiles.
risk_note: Usually low concern as food.

app_note: Menthol gives peppermint its cooling sensation.
risk_note: Concentrated mint oils differ from leaves.

app_note: Bay leaves are usually removed before eating because they stay tough.
risk_note: Whole leaves can be sharp; remove before serving.

app_note: Fennel seed has a sweet anise-like flavor.
risk_note: Allergy cross-reactivity claims need source review.

app_note: Cardamom is among the more expensive spices by weight.
risk_note: Usually used in small amounts.

app_note: Star anise is used in five-spice and some broths.
risk_note: Must not be confused with toxic Japanese star anise in sourcing contexts.

app_note: Saffron is costly because it is made from hand-harvested flower stigmas.
risk_note: Adulteration is common enough to consider source-quality notes.

app_note: Vanilla comes from an orchid and requires curing to develop aroma.
risk_note: Imitation vanilla should be categorized separately.

app_note: Garlic powder is dehydrated and ground garlic.
risk_note: High-FODMAP concern may matter for some users.

app_note: Onion powder gives savory sweetness and bulk flavor.
risk_note: High-FODMAP concern may matter for some users.
